lessons.title: wohnen — "to live," and your first regular verb
lessons.gloss: to live, to dwell — your first regular German verb

segments.text: Until now you have assembled fixed phrases. This chapter hands you the machine itself — and the first verb to run through it.
wohnen — "to live, to dwell."
Not to be alive — that is a different verb. Wohnen is where your bed is.
w-as-v — the w is an English v.
h-silent-lengthening — the h only stretches the o, exactly as in gehen and sehen.
So: VOH-nen, with a long open oh.
wohnen comes from Old High German wonēn, "to dwell, to be accustomed, to be content" — because dwelling somewhere and being used to it were the same idea.

That root survives in English, just barely, in wont: "as is his wont" means "as he is accustomed." It is also kin to win and wish — all from one root about striving for something, or being content with it.
So wohnen is not a stranger. It is the word behind wont, still doing the older job.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "wohnen" and English "wont" — accustomed, at home]

segments.text: What does wohnen mean? ("To live, to dwell.") Which English word is it? (Wont — accustomed.) What does the h do? (Only lengthens the o.)

lessons.title: der Stamm — drop the -en, and you have the machine
lessons.gloss: the stem — drop -en, and the endings have something to attach to

segments.text: You met the ending-swap on heißen. Here is the piece underneath it, and it is the reason the swap works on every verb.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the stem

segments.text: The stem is what is left when you take -en off the dictionary form.
wohnen minus -en leaves wohn-. That is the part that never changes. The endings attach to it, and the dictionary form you look up is simply the stem already wearing one of them.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the three singular endings

segments.text: Take wohn- and add:

utterances: Person: ich. Ending: -e. Form: ich wohne.
Person: du. Ending: -st. Form: du wohnst.

segments.text: You saw -e on ich heiße. The -st was hiding: heißen ends in ß, and ß + st collapses to heißt, so du heißt never showed you the s. On a normal stem it is plain — du wohnst.

This is not special to wohnen. Every regular verb in German runs exactly this, which is why learning one is learning thousands. Grammars call these weak verbs — "weak" because they take their endings meekly instead of changing their vowel the way strong verbs do. You will meet a strong one soon enough.
How do you get the stem? (Drop -en.) What is the stem of wohnen? (Wohn-.) Which endings go with ich and du? (-e and -st.) Why did du heißt not show the s? (ß and st collapse together.)

lessons.title: er, sie, es — "he," "she," "it," and one ending for all three
lessons.gloss: he, she, it — the three third-person pronouns, and the -t they share

segments.text: You can talk about yourself and to one other person. To talk about someone you need three more pronouns — and you already own one of them.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: er, sie, es

segments.text: er — "he." Said air, with the soft German r.
It pairs with the article you already know: der things are er things.
sie — "she." Said zee.

Yes: the same sound and spelling as the polite Sie, and as the sie meaning "they." German really does run three jobs through one word, and only the capital and the verb ending tell them apart. You will meet that properly later; for now, small sie with a -t ending means she.
The three pronouns line up with the three articles, which is the whole reason German bothers with genders:

utterances: Article: der. Pronoun: er. English: he.
Article: die. Pronoun: sie. English: she.
Article: das. Pronoun: es. English: it.

segments.text: One ending covers all three — attach -t to the stem:
er wohnt, sie wohnt, es wohnt.
English does the same thing with -s (he lives, she lives, it lives) and nowhere else in the paradigm. German's -t is that same odd little marker.

segments.instruction: "er wohnt", "sie wohnt", "es wohnt" — one ending, three people
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "er wohnt", "sie wohnt", "es wohnt" — one ending, three people]

segments.text: Which pronoun goes with der? (Er.) With die? (Sie.) What ending do all three take? (-t — er wohnt.) Which English ending does the same job? (-s, as in he lives.)

lessons.title: wir — "we," and an ending you have already been saying
lessons.gloss: we — and the ending that is the dictionary form again

segments.text: Three singular people down. Now the plural — and the first one is nearly free.
wir — "we." Said veer, with the w as a v and the soft trailing r, so it rhymes with mir and dir.
It is English we, wearing German pronunciation. Nothing else to learn.
Attach -en to the stem:
wir wohnen.
Which is the dictionary form, unchanged. German's infinitive and its wir form are identical, for every regular verb — so half of this ending was already in your head before you met it.
You have seen this once: Sie heißen, the polite form, is the same -en.

segments.instruction: "wohnen" then "wir wohnen" — the same word twice
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "wohnen" then "wir wohnen" — the same word twice]

segments.text: What does wir mean, and what does it rhyme with? ("We"; mir and dir.) Which ending does it take? (-en.) What else looks exactly like wir wohnen? (The dictionary form, wohnen.)

lessons.title: ihr — "you all," the plural English threw away
lessons.gloss: you all — the plural you English gave up

segments.text: Du is one friend. What if there are several? English has no clean answer any more. German does.
ihr — "you all," the plural of du.
Said eer: the h is silent and lengthens the i, the same trick as in Ihnen.
Use it for a group you would each call du — friends, family, a team. For a group of strangers you still use Sie.

English used to have this exact system and lost half of it. Thou was the singular and ye/you the plural — then thou faded, you took over both jobs, and English was left unable to say "you all" without inventing something: y'all, you guys, yous, you lot.
German never lost the distinction, so it needs no invention:

utterances: one person. Informal: du. Formal: Sie.
several people. Informal: ihr. Formal: Sie.

segments.text: Attach -t to the stem:
ihr wohnt.

The same -t as er wohnt. Two different people, one ending — so context, not the verb, tells you which is meant. That is the only place the German present tense is ever ambiguous, and the pronoun clears it up instantly.
The paradigm is now complete: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.

segments.instruction: "du wohnst" then "ihr wohnt" — one friend, then several
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "du wohnst" then "ihr wohnt" — one friend, then several]

segments.instruction: the whole six — wohne, wohnst, wohnt, wohnen, wohnt, wohnen
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the whole six — wohne, wohnst, wohnt, wohnen, wohnt, wohnen]

segments.text: What does ihr mean? ("You all.") Which English word did the same job before it was lost? (Ye — leaving y'all to fill the gap.) Which ending does ihr share, and with whom? (-t, with er/sie/es.)

lessons.title: The endings you can actually hear
lessons.gloss: why you can hear German endings, and cannot hear French ones

segments.text: You have all six endings. Before moving on, one fact about them that makes German easier than it looks.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: German endings are audible

segments.text: Say them aloud and they genuinely differ:
wohne, wohnst, wohnt, wohnen.

French writes just as many endings and pronounces almost none of them — parle, parles, parlent are three spellings of one sound. A French listener gets the person from the pronoun alone, because the verb tells them nothing.
German is the opposite. The verb carries real information, and you could very nearly tell who is speaking from the ending by itself.

That is worth knowing for two reasons. It makes listening easier than reading at first, and it makes the next question interesting: if German endings say who the subject is, why does German still insist on the pronoun? That is the end of this chapter.

segments.instruction: them again with your eyes closed, and hear the person change
segments.source: [YOU SAY: them again with your eyes closed, and hear the person change]
[YOU SAY: the full six in order]

segments.text: Are German verb endings audible? (Yes — wohne, wohnst, wohnt all differ.) And French ones? (Largely silent.) What does that let a German listener do? (Hear the person from the verb, not only the pronoun.)

lessons.title: in — the word that did not change
lessons.gloss: in — the same word as English in, and it needs no learning at all

segments.text: Ich wohne — I live. Live where? One more word and you have said something true about yourself.
in — "in."
Same spelling, same meaning, near enough the same sound: a short i as in English bit. This is one of the small handful of words German and English never bothered to change.
You have already met its neighbour auf ("on"). Between them they cover most of what English does with in and on.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: Ich wohne in …

segments.text: Put a place after it and the sentence is finished:
Ich wohne in Berlin. — "I live in Berlin."
Swap the city for your own and the sentence is yours. This is the first thing in this book you can say about your actual life without being handed the whole line.

segments.instruction: "in" — short i, exactly as in English
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "in" — short *i*, exactly as in English]

segments.instruction: the same sentence with the town you actually live in
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the same sentence with the town you actually live in]

segments.text: What does in mean? ("In" — unchanged.) Say where you live. (Ich wohne in …) Which word covers "on"? (Auf.)

lessons.title: wo — "where," and the German w-questions
lessons.gloss: where — the third of German's w-questions

segments.text: You can say where you live. To ask it, you need the question word — and it belongs to a family you have already started.
wo — "where." Said voh, a long oh.
Wo wohnst du? — "Where do you live?"
Note there is no extra "do" in German. English needs do to ask a question; German simply puts the question word first and the verb straight after it.
wo is English where with the -re worn away. And it is not alone — German's question words are the English ones with wh- flattened to w-:

utterances: wo means where.
wie means how.
wer means who.
wann means when.

segments.text: English spells them wh- and mostly says them w-; German just spells what it says. Once you spot the family, each new one costs almost nothing.
What does wo mean? ("Where.") Ask someone where they live. (Wo wohnst du?) What happened to English wh- in German? (It flattened to w-.)

lessons.title: machen — "to make," and it is exactly English make
lessons.gloss: to make, to do — and it is just English make

segments.text: Second verb — and it needs no new grammar at all. The stem-plus-ending machine you built on wohnen runs it unchanged.
machen — "to make," and also "to do." German uses one verb for both.
Stem: mach-. So ich mache, du machst, er macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie machen. Nothing new — that is the payoff of a regular pattern.
ch-ach — the ch after a is the raspy throat sound you met in Nacht, the ch of Scottish loch. Not the soft ich sound.
So: MAKH-en, with a clean open ah.
machen is English make, from Germanic makōn, "to shape, to fit together." The k became the ch rasp on the way, by the same High German consonant shift that gave you gut from good:

utterances: English: make. German: machen.
English: ik (old I). German: ich.
English: book. German: Buch.

segments.text: So machen is make, wearing German pronunciation.
What does machen mean? ("To make," and "to do.") Which English word is it? (Make.) Which ch does it use? (The raspy ach, not the soft ich.)

lessons.title: was — "what," and the t-to-s swap one last time
lessons.gloss: what — the fourth w-question, and the one you will use most

segments.text: You have wo. Here is its most useful sibling, and you can already predict how it is spelt.
was — "what." Said vass, short a, crisp s.
You met the rule that makes it: where English keeps a final t, German shows an s.

utterances: English: what. German: was.
English: that. German: das.
English: it. German: es.

segments.text: Third time you have seen this pair, and the last new word it gives you.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: Was machst du?

segments.text: Was machst du? — "What are you doing?"
Question word first, verb second, subject third — the same shape as Wo wohnst du?. And note again that German needs no "do": machst carries the whole question.
There is also no separate "am …-ing" form in German. Was machst du? covers both "what do you do?" and "what are you doing?" — context decides.

segments.instruction: "Was machst du?" then "Wo wohnst du?" — the same shape
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Was machst du?" then "Wo wohnst du?" — the same shape]

segments.text: What does was mean? ("What.") Which swap explains its spelling? (English t shows up as German s.) Ask what someone is doing. (Was machst du?)

lessons.title: lernen — "to learn," and its noun is lore
lessons.gloss: to learn — and its noun is English lore

segments.text: Third verb, same machine — and this is the one you are going to need to describe what you are doing right now.
lernen — "to learn."
Stem lern-: ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt. Three verbs now, one pattern.
r-uvular-german — the German r is a soft scrape at the back of the throat, nothing like the English r made with the tongue tip.
So: LER-nen, with a short e as in English bed.
lernen is English learn — the same Germanic root, barely disguised.

Its relatives are the good part. The German noun is die Lehre, "the teaching, the body of what is taught" — and that word is English lore. Folklore is the Lehre of a folk; the lore of a craft is what its learners have accumulated.
So German kept the verb and the noun in the same family, and English kept both too — it just stopped noticing that learn and lore were relatives.

segments.instruction: "lernen" (LER-nen) — scrape the r at the back
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "lernen" (*LER-nen*) — scrape the *r* at the back]

segments.text: What does lernen mean? ("To learn.") What is its noun, and which English word is that? (Die Lehre; lore.) Give the ich form. (Ich lerne.)

lessons.title: Deutsch — the language, and it means "of the people"
lessons.gloss: German, the language — and it means "of the people"

segments.text: One noun stands between you and a sentence about what you are doing right now — the name of the language itself.
Deutsch — "German," the language.
Capital D, because a language name is a noun and German capitalises every noun.
eu-diphthong — German eu is the oy of English boy.
tsch-ch — tsch is the tch of English match, the same cluster that opens tschüss.
So: DOYTCH, one syllable.

Deutsch comes from Old High German diutisc, "of the people, of the folk." The Germanic tribes simply called their own tongue the people's language — as opposed to Latin, the language of church and administration.
That root travelled a long way:

utterances: Word: Deutsch. Language: German. Route: diutisc, "of the people".
Word: Dutch. Language: English. Route: the same word, later narrowed to the Netherlands.
Word: Teutonic. Language: English. Route: via Latin Teutonicus.
Word: Tedesco. Language: Italian. Route: its own echo of diutisc.

segments.text: So English Dutch and German Deutsch are not lookalikes — they are one word that drifted apart, and English simply pointed it at a smaller country.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Deutsch" then "Dutch" — the same old word]
[YOU SAY: what it meant — "of the people"]

segments.text: What does Deutsch literally mean? ("Of the people.") Which English word is the same word? (Dutch.) Why the capital D? (It is a noun.)

lessons.title: Ich lerne Deutsch — your first real sentence
lessons.gloss: your first sentence built from parts, not handed to you whole

segments.text: Nothing new is coming. Every piece of the next line has had its own lesson — and that is exactly the point.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: Ich lerne Deutsch

segments.text: Ich lerne Deutsch. — "I am learning German."

utterances: Piece: ich. Where it came from: the introductions chapter.
Piece: lern-. Where it came from: the stem of lernen.
Piece: -e. Where it came from: the ich ending.
Piece: Deutsch. Where it came from: the last lesson.

segments.text: This is the first sentence in the book that was not handed to you. You built it: a pronoun, a stem, an ending, a noun. Change any piece and it still works.
Remember there is no separate "am …-ing" in German. Ich lerne covers both "I learn" and "I am learning," so this one line does the work of two English tenses.
The same slots take other words, and you already have all of them:
Ich wohne in Berlin., Was machst du?, Ich lerne Deutsch.
Three sentences, one machine. From here the language is combinations, not memorised lines.

segments.instruction: all three sentences in a row
segments.source: [YOU SAY: all three sentences in a row]

segments.text: Say "I am learning German." (Ich lerne Deutsch.) Which four pieces is it made of? (Ich, the stem lern-, the ending -e, and Deutsch.) How does German say "I am learning" as opposed to "I learn"? (It does not — ich lerne is both.)

lessons.title: Why German keeps the pronoun
lessons.gloss: why German keeps the pronoun even though its endings are audible

segments.text: Here is the puzzle left open earlier. German endings do say who the subject is. So why say ich at all?

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: three languages, three reasons

segments.text: Spanish, French and German each decide differently, and for different reasons:

utterances: Language: Spanish. The pronoun: dropped. Why: hablo already says "I".
Language: French. The pronoun: kept. Why: its endings are silent, so the pronoun is the only clue.
Language: German. The pronoun: kept. Why: its grammar demands an overt subject.

segments.text: The German reason is the interesting one, because it is not about sound. German endings are perfectly audible — you proved that a few lessons ago. The pronoun stays because a German sentence is built around the verb in second position, with something standing in front of it. Drop ich and there is nothing to hold that first slot.
So German keeps the pronoun for structure, French for sound, and Spanish keeps neither because it needs neither. Three answers, and only one of them is about being understood.

segments.instruction: the three reasons — Spanish drops, French keeps for sound, German keeps for structure

segments.instruction: "ich wohne", "ich mache", "ich lerne" — never without the ich
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ich wohne", "ich mache", "ich lerne" — never without the *ich*]

segments.text: Why does German keep the pronoun? (Its grammar needs an overt subject — the verb sits second, so something must come first.) Why does French? (Its endings are silent.) Why does Spanish not need to? (Hablo already says "I.")

lessons.title: Practice — building sentences, not reciting them
lessons.gloss: Chapter 5 payoff — building sentences from a pattern, not reciting them

segments.text: For the first time you are building German rather than repeating it. Run each verb through the three singular persons.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: three verbs, one pattern

utterances: Verb: wohnen. ich, du, er: wohne, wohnst, wohnt.
Verb: machen. ich, du, er: mache, machst, macht.
Verb: lernen. ich, du, er: lerne, lernst, lernt.

segments.text: The same endings every time — -e, -st, -t — and, unlike French, you can hear all three. You still keep the pronoun, because German needs an overt subject.

utterances: Wo wohnst du? means Where do you live?
Ich wohne in Berlin. Und du? means I live in Berlin. And you?
Ich wohne in Wien. Was machst du? means I live in Vienna. What are you doing?
Ich lerne Deutsch! means I'm learning German!
Sehr gut! means Very good!
Danke! — Bitte. means Thanks! — You're welcome.

segments.text: Every line is assembled from pieces you own. Nothing here was memorised whole.
